steps.role: Imagine… it happens + what that means
lines: Imagine: in a single night, the sea rises ten metres.
No storm. No warning. It just keeps rising.
You are standing on the quay of an old canal town.
Tonight the water climbs ten metres.
That is almost nine metres over your feet.
First you notice the sound.
The canal stops lapping, and begins to push.

steps.role: How people react; things in the street
lines: Traders carry their crates up to the bridge.
A horse is led to higher ground.
The boats rise with the water, until they float past the windows.

steps.role: One real fact with a number
lines: Today the sea is rising about four millimetres a year.
Ten metres would take two and a half thousand years.
The quay disappears.
Water walks into the square, past the statue, to the cellar doors.
Every doorstep here was built just above the sea it knew.
But nobody ever built for ten metres more.
By midnight, the water is above the front doors.
Then it stops, and it does not go back down.
When the light comes, the square is a lake.
Only rooftops and the mill are left.
The sea never attacked this town.
It only arrived.

derivations.explain: The sea rises 10 m, the quay is 1.2 m above the water, so 8.8 m stands over the quay.

reality.why_it_really_happens: The quay is 1.2 m above the canal, so after the first 1.2 m of rise the water flows over it and into the lower square.
The houses' front doors are 0.2–0.5 m above the street; at +8.8 m over the quay all ground floors are under. The rise stops because the scenario adds exactly 10 m.
Nothing removes the extra water, so the level stays; houses of 2–3 storeys (7–9 m) go under and only the taller roofs and the mill on the hill stay dry.
